bib.title: Chapter 5: Model Evaluation and Improvement
bib.venue: book chapter (Introduction to Machine Learning with Python, per directory name; not printed in the extracted text)

question: How should supervised models be evaluated and tuned: cross-validation, grid search and metrics beyond accuracy and R2?
contributions: Cross-validation variants (k-fold, stratified, leave-one-out, shuffle-split, group)
Grid search with CV, nested CV, parameter-grid analysis
Metrics for imbalanced binary, multiclass and regression, plus threshold/curve analysis and scoring parameter use

results.claim: Tuning SVC (C, gamma) on the test set reports 97% but the honest test score with a train/validation/test split is 92%.
results.setup: iris, 150 samples, split 112/38 then train/valid/test 84/28/38, SVC grid 6x6 over C and gamma
results.quote: So we can only claim to classify new data 92% correctly, not 97% correctly as we thought before!
results.note: Naive test-set search best score 0.97 (In[18]); validation-set search gave valid 0.96, test 0.92 (In[20]).

results.claim: Grid search with 5-fold CV on the training set then a single test evaluation gives 97% test accuracy.
results.setup: iris, train_test_split random_state=0 (112/38), GridSearchCV(SVC(), 6x6 grid, cv=5); best C=100, gamma=0.01

results.claim: Nested CV (5x5 stratified, 36-point grid) estimates SVC at 98% mean accuracy on iris, at a cost of 900 models.
results.setup: iris full 150 samples, inner and outer StratifiedKFold(5), 36 parameter combinations

results.claim: Grid search with 5-fold CV costs 36*5 = 180 model fits for the 6x6 grid.
Unstratified 3-fold CV on class-ordered iris gives zero accuracy in every fold.
Default 3-fold CV on iris with logistic regression gives 0.961, 0.922, 0.958; 5-fold mean is 0.96.
Leave-one-out on iris runs 150 iterations and gives 0.95 mean accuracy.
Grid search cv_results_ shows SVC accuracy ranges from about 40% to 96% across the C/gamma grid.
results.setup: iris, SVC RBF, 6x6 grid C and gamma in 0.001..100, cv=5
results.note: Low end: 'around 40%' in text; mean_test_score 0.366 in Table of In[31].

results.claim: A majority-class dummy classifier gets about 90% accuracy on the 9-vs-rest digits task, while a depth-2 tree gets 92% and logistic regression 98%.
results.setup: digits, y = target==9, train_test_split random_state=0, test n=450 (403 negative, 47 positive)

results.claim: Confusion matrix for logistic regression on 9-vs-rest: TN 401, FP 2, FN 8, TP 39.
F1 separates models that accuracy barely distinguishes: majority 0.00, dummy 0.10, tree 0.55, logistic regression 0.89.
results.note: Text later says dummy f-score is 0.13 on the nine class (p286) while In[45] and the report print 0.10.

results.claim: Logistic regression classification report for 'nine': precision 0.95, recall 0.83, f1 0.89 on support 47.
Lowering the SVC decision threshold from 0 to -0.8 raised class-1 recall from 0.67 to 1.00 and cut precision from 0.35 to 0.32.

AUC for random forest 0.937 vs SVC 0.916 on the same imbalanced blobs.

results.claim: Three SVMs with identical 90% accuracy on 9-vs-rest have AUC 0.50, 0.90, 1.00 for gamma 1, 0.05, 0.01.
results.note: Text prose says gamma=1.0 AUC 'chance level' and gamma=0.05 'drastically improves to an AUC of 0.5', which contradicts the printed 0.90.

results.quote: Predicting randomly always produces an AUC of 0.5, no matter how imbalanced the classes in a dataset are.

Selecting gamma by AUC (0.01) beats selecting by accuracy (0.0001) on both test AUC and test accuracy.

limits: Small toy datasets (iris 150, digits 450 test), single splits; no variance or significance on the metric comparisons.
Code uses old scikit-learn API (n_iter, sklearn.metrics.scorer SCORERS, 'mean_squared_error' scorer names, 'avg / total' reports); modern names are neg_mean_squared_error, n_splits, get_scorer_names.
Text inconsistencies: prose says gamma=0.05 AUC 0.5 while output is 0.90; dummy f-score 0.13 in prose vs 0.10 in output; In[17]/In[16] and In[34]/In[35] numbering duplicates.
Calibration and cost-sensitive evaluation are only mentioned, not covered; regression metrics get one paragraph.
practices: Hold out a test set used once; select models and parameters on a validation set or by cross-validation on the training set (p262-263, p266, p302).
Use stratified k-fold for classification and plain k-fold for regression, which is the scikit-learn default; shuffle with a fixed random_state if the data is ordered (p255-257).
Use GroupKFold when samples from the same patient/speaker/person must not span train and test (p259-260).
Start with a coarse grid, inspect cv_results_ as a heat map, and widen the range if the optimum is on an edge; never tune ranges on the test set (p267-271).
Use a list of dicts as param_grid for conditional parameters such as kernel (p271).
Use nested CV only to assess how well a model class generalizes on a dataset, not to produce a model (p273).
Grid search and CV are embarrassingly parallel: set n_jobs, but do not nest n_jobs inside the estimator (p274-275).
Choose the metric closest to the business goal; accuracy misleads on imbalanced data, so compare against DummyClassifier baselines (p275-279).
Use precision when false positives are costly, recall when false negatives are costly, F1 to combine; look at the confusion matrix first (p283-285).
Tune the decision threshold on a validation set, never the test set; fix an operating point such as 90% recall (p288-289).
Prefer AUC or average precision over accuracy for imbalanced data and model selection, and pass scores (decision_function/predict_proba), not predictions (p292-297, p300).
For multiclass imbalance use macro F1 to weight classes equally, micro F1 to weight samples equally (p299).
Pass scoring= to GridSearchCV and cross_val_score to select by the metric you care about (p300-301).

terms.definition: the data is first partitioned into five parts of (approximately) equal size, called folds, each used once as test set
we split the data such that the proportions between classes are the same in each fold as they are in the whole dataset
each split samples train_size many points for the training set and test_size many (disjoint) points for the test set, repeated n_splits times
an outer loop over train/test splits, with a grid search run inside each outer training set; the result is a list of scores, not a model
the set used to select the parameters of the model, between training and test
incorrect positive prediction / incorrect negative prediction (type I / type II error)
TP/(TP+FP), how many predicted positives are actually positive (PPV)
TP/(TP+FN), how many positives are captured (sensitivity, hit rate, TPR)
area under the ROC curve; probability that a random positive scores higher than a random negative
a requirement such as 90% recall set on a classifier
a calibrated model provides an accurate measure of its uncertainty
macro = unweighted per-class mean; weighted = support-weighted; micro = pooled TP/FP/FN counts
